'''Joseph E. Coleman''' (1922-2000) was an American politician, attorney and chemist. He was a member of the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]].

==Early life==
Coleman was born in 1922, and grew up in [[Mississippi]] during a time in which the southern United States was dominated by racial segregation and [[Jim Crow laws|the Jim Crow laws]].<ref name=Death/> In 1948, he became the first African-American to earn a degree, a [[B.S.]] in chemistry, from [[Albright College]].<ref name=Nelson1968>{{cite news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/philadelphia-daily-news-joseph-e-colema/202072383/ |title=Joseph E. Coleman: Chemist, Lawyer, City Planner |first=Nels |last=Nelson |work=[[Philadelphia Daily News]] |date=March 4, 1968 |via=newspapers.com }}</ref> He went on to work as a research chemist, patent attorney and author.<ref name=Albright>{{cite web|last=Post-Stoudt|first=Jennifer|title=Being African American at Albright|url=http://www.albright.edu/reporter/fall01/afamexp1.html|work=The Albright Reporter (Fall 2001, Volume 21, Number 4)|publisher=Albright College|accessdate=November 26, 2011}}</ref>

==City council==
In 1971, Coleman was elected to be president of the [[Philadelphia City Council]], representing the Eighth District.<ref name=Death />

===Presidency===
In June 1980, incumbent Council President [[George X. Schwartz|George Schwartz]] was implicated in the [[Abscam|Abscam scandal]], and resigned. Coleman became Acting Council President, and was unanimously elected to the post when Council reconvened in October.<ref name=ActingPresident /><ref name=PresidentElection /> He became the first African-American elected to the post in the city's history.<ref name=Library>{{cite web|title=Joseph E. Coleman Northwest Regional Library: Branch History|url=http://libwww.freelibrary.org/branches/history.cfm?loc=NWR|publisher=The Free Library of Philadelphia|accessdate=November 26, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120126031506/https://libwww.freelibrary.org/branches/history.cfm?loc=NWR|archive-date=January 26, 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref>

As President, Coleman sought to maintain a more conciliatory atmosphere than the more combative Schwartz.<ref name=Death /> [[Anna Verna]], a close friend and colleague of Coleman's (who went on to become the City Council's first female President in 1999), characterized Coleman's leadership style as "calm".<ref name=Death /> He also sought to clean up the Council's image in the wake of Abscam,<ref name=PresidentElection /> while dramatically increasing the Council's oversight of [[Mayor of Philadelphia|Mayoral]] projects and plans.<ref name=Death />

He saw-off a challenge to his presidency following the 1987 elections, when [[Joan L. Krajewski|Joan Krajewski]], also a Democrat, sought to unseat him.<ref name=Challenge>{{cite news|last=Clark|first=Robin|title=Krajewski Announces Bid For Council Helm|url=http://articles.philly.com/1987-11-07/news/26175260_1_krajewski-joe-coleman-council-president|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130131105725/http://articles.philly.com/1987-11-07/news/26175260_1_krajewski-joe-coleman-council-president|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 31, 2013|accessdate=November 26, 2011|newspaper=The Philadelphia Inquirer|date=November 7, 1987}}</ref>

===Retirement===
After surviving a tough re-election contest in 1987, in which the ''[[Philadelphia Inquirer]]'' strongly endorsed his [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] opponent,<ref name=LastCampaign>{{cite news|title=District Council Races: Replace Joseph Coleman|url=http://articles.philly.com/1987-10-21/news/26214123_1_political-newcomer-council-members-district-council-races|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304062031/http://articles.philly.com/1987-10-21/news/26214123_1_political-newcomer-council-members-district-council-races|url-status=dead|archive-date=March 4, 2016|accessdate=November 26, 2011|newspaper=The Philadelphia Inquirer|date=October 21, 1987}}</ref> Coleman announced that he would not seek re-election on February 14, 1991.<ref ==Personal life==
Coleman was married, and had three children—a son and two daughters. In September 1997, his daughter, Stephanie Coleman Epps, was shot to death in front of her two children by a former boyfriend. Coleman, who was suffering from the effects of [[diabetes]], was unable to attend the trial, though the man was convicted of the murder and sentenced to death in December of that year.<ref name=Death />

==Death and honors==
On December 31, 2000, Coleman died in the [[Mount Airy, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania|Mount Airy]] home he shared with his wife, Jessie.<ref name=Death />

The Community Education Centers named its [[Philadelphia, Pennsylvania|Philadelphia-area]] treatment center after Coleman. The Center's clients are referred through the [[Pennsylvania]] Department of Corrections, the Pennsylvania Board of Probation and Parole, or the [[Bucks County, Pennsylvania|Bucks County]] Department of Corrections. The Center, named Coleman Hall, provides an array of residential reentry treatment services designed to reduce recidivism.<ref name=ColemanHall>{{cite web|title=Coleman Hall|url=http://www.cecintl.com/facilities_rr_pa_003.html|publisher=Community Education Centers|accessdate=November 26, 2011}}</ref> In 2002, the Philadelphia Free Library system's Northwest Regional Library, located in [[Germantown, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania|Germantown]], was renamed the Joseph E. Coleman Northwest Regional Library.<ref name=Library />

Albright College also created a scholarship award in Coleman's honor. The Distinguished Joseph E. Coleman Award provides financial assistance ranging from $8,000 to $12,000 to African-American students that show academic excellence as well as community and/or extracurricular involvement.<ref name=Albright />
